newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian regional plan,consessions to woo investors.
newsitem.headline: Serbian regional plan,consessions to woo investors.

text.p: Serbia on Wednesday presented an abridged version of its regional development plan until 2010, hoping it will increase foreign investment by defining prospects and optimal conditions for the use of its territory.
"We expect the plan along with the earlier adopted law on consessions to attract foreign interest in big investment projects," said Construction Minister Branislav Ivkovic.
He said this was the first comprehensive document providing long-term guidelines on Serbia's regional development to show potential investors where and how much it was possible to invest.
"The plan proves that (investment) projects are rational, justified and profitable," he said.
Under the law on the management of natural resources by domestic and foreign companies, the government will grant consessions for exploration and exploitation of mineral ores.
The law, passed early in May, also envisages construction, maintainance and use of energy facilities, gas and oil pipelines, roads, railways, telecommunications, airports and other utilities.
"The law on consessions allows all those who invest here to cover their investment and make a profit," Ivkovic said.
But future investments had to help further development of the country and must be environmentally friendly, he added.
He said foreign interest had increased significantly. The
most interest was shown in a planned highway from Nis in south Serbia to the Macedonian border and in investments in waterworks and the power and oil industries.

Ile Kovacevic, director of the Yugoslav survey consulting firm, said foreign investors were already present but were only doing market research monitoring to find out about economic and legislative stability.
Since war-related U.N. sanctions were suspended in November 1995 until the end of June this year, 1,583 diverse foreign investment contracts were signed in Yugoslavia, Kovacevic said.
He gave no detaials of their value, but said they ranged from a few hundred thousand to one million German marks.

One Western analyst, who asked not to be named, said significant foreign capital was unlikely to flow into the country before its full return to the international political and financial organisations.
